summary: Pharaoh's uninterpreted dreams bring Joseph out of prison, and Joseph predicts seven abundant years followed by seven years of severe famine. He proposes storing food, is appointed second over Egypt, and is portrayed as an impartial ruler; the chapter closes with the abundant harvests and stores accumulated under his administration.
whyItMatters: Joseph's interpretation becomes a practical plan for survival and transforms his position from prisoner to administrator. The account emphasizes his integrity as well as his exceptional authority.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Pharaoh's court and the Egyptian cities during the transition into the seven years of abundance.
context.literaryForm: Dream-interpretation and promotion narrative followed by an idealized portrait of governance and harvest collection.

before.text: The restored butler has forgotten Joseph after Joseph correctly interpreted his prison dream. Pharaoh's new dreams provide the occasion to remember him.

here.text: The chapter joins interpretation, planning, public appointment, and food collection as stages of Joseph's rise.

after.text: The next chapter turns to Judah and Tamar and ends by locating their story at the completion of the abundant years.

outline.heading: Dreams and an agricultural plan
outline.note: Joseph interprets the two dreams as one sequence of abundance and famine and recommends storage.

outline.heading: Public appointment over Egypt
outline.note: Pharaoh recognizes Joseph’s wisdom and grants him rank, clothing, insignia, and authority.

outline.heading: The character of Joseph’s rule
outline.note: The narrator praises impartiality, freedom from bribery and pride, and peace.

outline.heading: Name, marriage, age, and gathering
outline.note: Royal integration and chronology lead into extraordinary harvests and full granaries.

keyVerses.text: And now let Pharaoh appoint overseers in all the land of Egypt, and let them store up food in every city throughout the days of the years of plenty, and there will be food for the seven years of famine, and the land will not perish through the famine, for it will be very severe.'
keyVerses.why: Joseph’s response to the predicted famine includes concrete city-by-city preparation.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph ruled over all the land of Egypt, and all the princes of Pharaoh, and all his servants, and all who did the king's business loved him, for he walked in uprightness, for he was without pride and arrogance, and he had no respect of persons, and did not accept gifts, but he judged in uprightness all the people of the land.
keyVerses.why: The chapter defines upright rule through impartiality and refusal of gifts as well as humility.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph gathered food into every city until they were full of corn until they could no longer count and measure it for its multitude.
keyVerses.why: The final image of full stores shows the proposed preparation being carried out.

questions.question: Are Pharaoh’s two dreams interpreted separately?
questions.answer: Joseph says they are one: both concern seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine. The chapter summarizes their meaning without retelling the dream images themselves.

questions.question: What does Joseph recommend doing with the warning?
questions.answer: He recommends overseers throughout Egypt who will collect food in each city during the plentiful years. The aim stated in the speech is to prevent the land from perishing when the severe famine arrives.

questions.question: What shows the extent of Joseph’s authority?
questions.answer: He receives the second chariot, fine garments, a chain, and a ring, with a public proclamation of his new status. Pharaoh says only the throne will remain above him.

questions.question: What are “byssus garments”?
questions.answer: They are the ceremonial garments used here to mark Joseph's elevated court position. Their role in the scene is to signal status, alongside the gold chain and ring.

questions.question: What qualities make Joseph a good ruler in this account?
questions.answer: The narrator says he lacks pride, does not favor persons, refuses gifts, and judges uprightly. The description places ethical conduct beside wisdom and royal power rather than treating promotion alone as proof of good leadership.

questions.question: Should the statement that no evil person remained be treated as a census result?
questions.answer: The claim belongs to the chapter's sweeping portrayal of an orderly and peaceful kingdom under Joseph. It does not provide evidence about every Egyptian individual's conduct, and its emphatic praise should be read as narrative rhetoric.

questions.question: How does the chapter connect Joseph’s elevation to the wider family chronology?
questions.answer: It says he is thirty when he stands before Pharaoh and that Isaac dies in that year. The closing harvest report then shows the seven abundant years beginning as Joseph predicted.

glossary.def: The material of the garments Joseph receives as part of the public signs of his appointment.
Officials Joseph proposes appointing across Egypt to organize food storage before the famine.
Favoritism in judgment, which the narrator says Joseph avoids.
